part_title: Machine Learning Lifecycle — From Business Goals to Monitoring
review_basis: Original AIF Module 03 WebP slides 54–58 individually viewed and narrated in their actual diagram order, including numeric examples and bottom decision cues.

scenes.title: The ML lifecycle: complete overview
scenes.narration: This picture shows the complete machine learning lifecycle. Think of a retailer that wants to sort product photos automatically. Start at the first box: define and frame the business problem. We must state what successful classification means before choosing any algorithm. Arrow two leads to data preparation: collect relevant labelled images, fix mistakes, and make useful features. In the third box, build, train, tune, and evaluate a model. Training means learning patterns from examples; evaluation means checking those patterns against examples the model did not learn from. Fourth, deploy and predict: make the trained system available to the store's application. Fifth, monitor and improve: watch actual prediction quality and changes in incoming images. Now follow the lower blue return arrow and its decision diamond. If business goals are not met, revisit data, features, or the model and train again. If goals are met, deliver value and keep monitoring. The three bottom panels reinforce this same retail example, the main concern at each step, and the decision cue. A model is not finished merely because training succeeds. Check your understanding: if accuracy falls after a new product category appears, is the lifecycle over? No. Investigate the new data and retrain or adjust the system as necessary.

scenes.title: ML lifecycle: business goals and problem framing
scenes.narration: Read these four panels from left to right. First, business stakeholders define the outcome, the available resources, and a measurable success target. In the online retail example at the bottom, the goal is to retain more customers and grow revenue. The key performance indicator, or K P I, may be the churn rate, which is the share of customers who stop using the service. Second, translate the business question into a machine learning task: predict which customers are likely to leave. Notice this is a prediction about customers, not a guarantee that a customer will leave. Third, decide whether learning from data is actually appropriate. The green sign says use machine learning when patterns in data can improve outcomes. The orange sign says consider simple rules or an existing system when they are sufficient. Fourth, assemble the right team: the stakeholder defines success, the data scientist frames the prediction, the data engineer prepares reliable data, the machine learning architect designs the overall solution, and the subject expert explains the business context. A prediction alone cannot retain a customer; the business must act on the result. Quick decision: should we train a model before deciding how success will be measured? No. Agree on the business outcome and measurement first.

scenes.title: ML lifecycle: data preparation and training
scenes.narration: Follow the blue arrows across the four numbered stages. At stage one, collect and integrate data from places such as customer records, account activity, and support messages into a usable dataset. Integration means making these pieces consistent enough to analyze together. Stage two is cleaning and exploration. Missing values, inconsistent formats, and unusual observations can mislead a model, so inspect tables and charts before training. Stage three engineers features: information that helps the model recognize relevant patterns. The centre picture moves from original data to transformed and derived features. For customer churn, examples could include the number of days since the last login and recent usage trends. Stage four trains, tunes, and evaluates the model. Training updates what the model has learned. Tuning selects settings, and evaluation checks whether predictions work on held-out data. Notice the long feedback arrow under the stages. The process repeats when evaluation shows weaknesses. The example at the bottom connects customer information, activity and support interactions to a churn prediction. The decision box says check data quality and useful features before assuming that simply changing a model will solve poor results. A useful question: can a highly sophisticated algorithm recover missing customer history by itself? No. Reliable, relevant data is the foundation.

scenes.title: Exploratory data analysis
scenes.narration: This slide shows exploratory data analysis, often shortened to E D A. It means examining information before training a model to find patterns, errors, and possible predictive features. Start at the left with the example table: hours studied, test score, hours slept, and distractions. The rows are individual observations, and columns are variables. Next, move right to the scatter plot. The horizontal axis is hours studied and the vertical axis is test score. The upward trend suggests an association, but a trend does not prove that study hours caused every score difference. The two small histograms show the distributions of test scores and sleep hours. Now inspect the correlation matrix. A correlation near positive one indicates variables tend to rise together; near negative one indicates one tends to fall as the other rises. Here hours studied and test score have a displayed correlation of zero point eight five. Study hours and distractions have minus zero point six. Sleep hours and test score have a smaller positive zero point three. On the right the slide identifies study time, sleep and distractions as candidate features. The bottom decision cue suggests that very highly correlated features may be redundant, but do not remove them automatically: consider the model and business meaning first. Check: does zero point eight five mean an eighty-five percent chance that studying causes a high mark? No. Correlation is not a causal probability.

scenes.title: ML lifecycle: deployment, monitoring and retraining
scenes.narration: We have trained and tested a model. What happens after that? Follow the three large panels: deployment, monitoring, and retraining. On the left, new live data flows into a trained model, and predictions flow out to an application used by real people. Deployment simply means making the model available for actual use. The lower left box reminds us to choose a suitable option, such as real-time, batch, asynchronous or serverless prediction; the right choice depends on workload and response time needs. In the middle is monitoring. The chart and warning marker emphasize that we must observe performance, incoming data quality, unexpected model behavior, errors and data drift. Drift means that the new data, or the relationship between data and outcomes, changes compared with the conditions during training. On the right, new images, records and tables feed a retraining cycle. Retraining is not just pressing a button; use reviewed data, compare performance, and redeploy only when the updated model passes appropriate tests. The bottom example is an online store recommending products while customer tastes change. Follow the long lower arrow back to deployment: this cycle is continuous. Decision check: if recommendations become less useful even though the API still responds, is production monitoring successful? Not yet. We must check prediction quality, not merely service availability.
